title: Bankruptcy Watch
content:
Clients, Investors, and Friends,

According to Co-pilot, Microsoft’s AI offering, six businesses related to Donald J. Trump have declared bankruptcy, all Chapter 11 filings, which meant the debt was restructured while the businesses were allowed to continue operations. They were all casino and hotel related businesses, and don’t include any of other enterprises that were either voluntarily or involuntarily shut down, such as Trump Mortgage, Trump University, Trump Foundation, etc.

As such, it seems simultaneously ironic and apropos that despite all his personal flaws, he was re-elected for his perceived economic and business acumen, yet might oversee the largest bankruptcy in history, that of the United States federal government.

I know that is an extreme statement, and to be perfectly clear, I am not blaming the current administration. But, please don’t fall for the political rhetoric – it has not mattered one iota what party was in charge. For 30 years, our government has been driving toward the fiscal cliff, and all combinations of power have simply ignored it. However, Trump campaigned that he was the only one that could stop us from going over, yet his policies all seem to be hitting the accelerator. So, it just seems like karma is warming up.

As shown in the prior chart, up until the Great Recession, our GDP growth generally benefited from incremental federal debt. In fact, leading to the dot.com bubble, the economy was humming, tax revenue was growing healthily, and federal debt issuance slowed to a meager 2% growth rate. With the new debt issuance so low, the ratio of GDP growth to new debt surged.

However, since the Great Recession in 2008, we have not had a single 5-year cycle where our GDP grew more than our federal debt, as the ratio has remained below $1. During the Great Recession and COVID years, lack of economic growth combined with surging government debt caused this ratio to plummet. Borrowing $1 and getting $0.24 of economic growth in return is not a recipe for long term economic health.

Recall the chart that I frequently referred to as the scariest one in my deck, which shows that our government’s ability to pay interest on its debt is deteriorating rapidly. Not only is new debt being issued to fund current deficits, but maturing debt is being refinanced at much higher rates. In fact, interest on US treasury debt is the third largest spending category of the federal government behind only Medicare and Social Security. In the last 12 months, net interest on the federal debt used up almost 20% of every tax dollar collected, another modern era high.

We had a short-term pause in this metric due to the government shutdown and thus no new debt was issued. However, after those political issues were resolved, the upward trajectory resumed (green circle). We know with nearly 100% certainty that the US government will continue to borrow more to fund the structural fiscal deficits (dotted black line). Thus, the only potential relief would be lower cost of debt via lower interest rates. That’s certainly one reason why the current administration argues for lower interest rates at every opportunity. Unfortunately, persistent inflation is preventing that from happening.

The US Federal Reserve (the “Fed”) and the US Treasury are already trying to do what they can to delay reaching the edge. However, their tools are quite limited considering the magnitude of the problem. Recall quantitative easing (QE), when the Fed magically created trillions of dollars to purchase US treasuries and other publicly traded debt to keep interest rates low and markets functioning. Post-COVID, the Fed was methodically reducing that support. But, rather quietly, the Fed’s balance sheet has been slowly growing again. All else equal, with incremental demand from the Fed, US treasury prices should be supported, and interest rates should stay contained. Of course, not all else is equal, as our isolationist policies are reducing the demand for US treasuries by the rest of the world.

As for the US Treasury, Secretary Bessent has been quite active lately. A couple weeks ago, there was a coordinated effort with Japan to stabilize the falling yen. But rather than using US dollars, which would require selling US treasuries resulting in upward pressure on US rates, the US Treasury used euros. More recently, Secretary Bessent announced an accelerated buyback of government debt that could be higher than $4B. Since longer term rates are higher than shorter term rates, it makes sense to do so to save on interest costs. Not so ironically, private investor Bessent frequently criticized such moves by his predecessors. Nonetheless, the market’s knee-jerk reaction was a sharp drop in long-term rates. However, after realizing that it’s a drop in the ocean of debt, yields jumped back up the following day.

After decades of fiscal mismanagement, there are no easy answers. Our annual deficits have become structural, such that the top three categories of spending (Medicare, social security, and interest) already exhaust all the revenue collected, which means the US government must borrow to pay for every other expense, such as the military and all discretionary spending. Further, it’s only going to get worse as baby boomers continue to enroll in social security and Medicare and interest costs continue to climb. Keep in mind, the Congressional Budget Office expects both Medicare and Social Security to be underfunded in 2033 and 2032, respectively, both well within the vitally important 10-yr treasury time frame. Investors will undoubtedly want to be compensated more via higher rates (lower bond prices) as those dates get closer.

The most likely scenario, in my view, is that the market will continue to price in the deteriorating creditworthiness of the US government, and longer-term interest rates will rise, which will force both the Fed and US Treasury to ramp up their money creation to try to keep interest rates contained. Based on history, those efforts will likely fail, and in fact, might cause rates to accelerate higher due to the inflationary pressures they will cause. That will cause even further intervention, and so on, and so on.

It will not likely be a default in the literal sense of the word. I expect that US debt holders will still get paid what they were promised with US dollars. However, the value and purchasing power of those dollars is very likely going to be much less as significantly more dollars are put into the economy. As such, we will continue to stay away from long-term debt and have a healthy exposure to gold, precious metals, and other investments that should benefit from a weaker US dollar.

Thank you for your time, support, and trust,

Craig Peterman, CFA, CFP®
Managing Director

title: 2nd Quarter 2026 Market Update
content:
Clients, Investors, and Friends,

About twenty-seven years ago, a new and powerful technology was taking the world by storm. Everything in our lives was going to change, and millionaires were made overnight simply by creating a business that was based on this new technology. Money was thrown at these businesses regardless of their business plan, proof of concept, or any reasonable estimate of when investors would start to see a return on their investment.

That new technology was the internet, of course, and without question, it changed all our lives, which led to the creation of several new industries (e.g. smart phones) and a much more interconnected world. That part of the investment thesis proved 100% correct. Unfortunately for most investors, especially those late to the game, the financial repercussions were equally as influential, but to the downside.

Fast forward to today, and our current AI driven euphoria seems similar in many ways. Money is being thrown at participants with few strings attached, billionaires are being created overnight, and the actual investment economics are full of uncertainties that are being ignored. The promise of productivity gains sounds eerily familiar as the bulls continue to justify the seemingly endless availability of capital.

More specifically related to financial markets, the optimism priced into existing market prices can be evaluated by looking at any of the myriads of valuation metrics, a few of which we have explored in prior recaps. Over the last several years, the conclusion has generally been the same — large cap stocks, represented by the S&P 500 Index, has traded at incredibly high premiums, which also means expectations for future growth have been extremely high.

In fact, looking at a widely respected long-term valuation model, the Shiller P/E ratio currently shows that the S&P 500 is trading at the highest premium since the dot.com bubble. The model has earned its reputation because it incorporates 10 years of inflation adjusted earnings, which smooths out short-term aberrations. Always keep in mind, valuation metrics should never be used as timing tools. As the industry saying goes, the market can be irrational longer than you can remain solvent. However, valuation measures can be used to evaluate the risks associated with investing at today's market prices.

Cyclically Adjusted Price/Earnings (CAPE) or Shiller P/E

With signs of gambling and irrational investment behavior everywhere, not just in premium valuations, market participants were also greeted with its first macro surprise, such that newly appointed US Federal Reserve Chairman Warsh was not nearly as dovish (think loose monetary policy) as the market thought a Trump appointee would be. In fact, since his appointment in May, his public focus has been on taming inflation, which generally means keeping short term rates high or even raising them. After all, US inflation has consistently been above average since coming out of the COVID years, and it has been accelerating lately.

Unfortunately for the incoming Chairman, it is uncertain if the monetary tools at his disposal will be sufficient to reign in inflation without triggering a significant reduction in demand. All our major non-monetary policies of the last few years have been inflationary, including tariffs, reduced immigration, and the conflict with Iran, all of which reduced the supply of goods and services. From Econ 101, all else equal, lower supply results in higher prices.

Add in the insatiable demand from AI infrastructure, the largest capital expenditure cycle ever, the costly combo of high demand and lower supply could be a difficult trend to break.

To make matters more precarious, the average US consumer is already feeling the pinch. Not only has job growth slowed, but the number of citizens leaving the workforce has recently picked up, adding to a significant divergence in the reported data. If one only looks at the official unemployment rate, it was already low and has been trending lower (red line — inverse scale). However, if one looks at the percentage of able-bodied citizens that are working, the trend has clearly been in the opposite direction (blue line).

Unfortunately for the economy, this trend has two major implications. The more obvious one has been the slowdown in consumer income and spending. Despite the incredible AI capital investments underway, US consumer spending still represents roughly 70% of the US economy. Thus, as the post-COVID free money and pent-up surge dissipates, disposable income and thus retail sales have been decelerating in tandem.

The less obvious impact from a shrinking workforce is more inflation, as employers have to pay more to keep the workers they have and/or produce less. I'm guessing everyone reading this has experienced longer wait times, less customer service, and more issues related to their purchases. Automation and now AI are expected to improve our productivity. In some cases, absolutely (e.g. free 1-day delivery). In others (e.g. customer service), not so much.

As mentioned in a prior recap, we just might be entering a most unusual economic environment called stagflation. The overall economy has been decelerating, but the price pressures remain elevated due to fiscal and geopolitical policies. The top 20% are doing great primarily due to rising asset prices, but the bottom 80% are feeling the stress paycheck to paycheck. Unless Federal Reserve Chairman Warsh has a magic bullet, it is going to be a difficult task to meet his goal of finally bringing down inflation to acceptable levels (2% range) without tipping more consumers and the economy over the edge. With so much optimism priced in by premium stock valuations, the stakes couldn't be higher because if the top 20% start pulling back on spending, there's no telling how severe the next economic downturn could be.

Thank you for your time, support, and trust,

Craig Peterman, CFA, CFP®
Managing Director
